t: 3750 - Minimum Number of Flips to Reverse Binary String
o:
We must transform the binary representation of n into the reverse of its original form; the target is fixed. The minimum number of bit flips to turn string s into target t is simply the number of positions where they differ (each differing bit needs exactly one flip, matching bits need zero). So the answer is the Hamming distance between s and reversed(s).

Example 1: '111' reversed is '111' — zero mismatches, answer 0. Example 2: '1010' vs '0101' differs in all 4 positions, answer 4. Note mismatches always come in symmetric pairs (except possibly the middle bit, which can never mismatch itself), but counting directly is simplest.
k: Minimum flips between two fixed strings = Hamming distance
Answer = number of indices i with s[i] != s[len-1-i] (equivalently popcount(s XOR reverse(s)))
No optimization is possible — the target is fixed, unlike 'flip to make palindrome' variants

a.n: Approach 1: Hamming Distance via Two Pointers
a.i: Build the binary string, then compare position i with position n-1-i for the first half; each unequal pair contributes exactly one flip per side, i.e., count both sides or count i over the full string.
s: Convert n to its binary string without leading zeros
Count indices i in [0, len) where s[i] != s[len-1-i]
a.t: O(log n) — the binary string has log₂n + 1 bits
a.sp: O(log n) — the string (O(1) possible comparing extracted bits arithmetically)

w: This is a direct application of Hamming distance; distinguish it carefully from the classic 'minimum flips to make s a palindrome' (where you'd count mismatched pairs and halve). Here the target is the reversal of the original, so every mismatched pair costs 2 flips, which the full-string count captures automatically. Follow-up: minimum flips to make s itself a palindrome, or to make s equal to the reversal of a different number.
